strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: GPU overprovisioning for online LLM serving and the opportunity to harvest stranded resources for offline (best-effort) inference, which is increasingly relevant with compound AI systems.

The motivation is supported by concrete evidence: real-world BurstGPT trace analysis (Figure 1) and a controlled experiment showing that naïve priority-based colocation on vLLM increases P99 TTFT by ~60× (Figure 2), clearly establishing why existing systems fall short.

The design is coherent and technically sound: layer-granularity preemption via safepoints (with a reasoned granularity trade-off analysis), incremental asynchronous KV cache checkpointing that exploits the statelessness of LLM inference, background prefetching to overlap swap-in with compute, and an SLO-aware profiler-driven scheduler.

The implementation atop vLLM (4165 lines of code) is substantive, including priority queues, safepoint instrumentation, extended KV cache manager with GPU-CPU block mapping, and dual CUDA streams for overlapped swap I/O.

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive: end-to-end comparison on a real trace, ON/OFF phased load patterns, robustness sweeps over burstiness (CV) and request rates, and an ablation drill-down (Figure 8) that quantifies each component's contribution, plus measurement of preemption responsiveness (5.41ms) and safepoint overhead (~4%).
weaknesses: The evaluation is limited to a single model (Llama-2-7B) on a single A100-40G GPU, despite claims of generalization (e.g., that layer sizes 'do not vary much' across LLMs, support for tensor/pipeline parallelism, multiple GPUs, long-context scenarios, PEFT models). None of these generality claims are empirically validated; multi-GPU and multi-model experiments are absent.

Baselines are weak: the main comparison is against vLLM 0.4.2 (an older version) and a self-constructed 'vLLM++' strawman. No head-to-head comparison with recent co-serving or disaggregated systems such as Sarathi-Serve, DistServe, Splitwise, Llumnix, or S3, some of which directly target the throughput-latency trade-off the paper claims to resolve. The headline 2.35× and 84× numbers therefore are hard to contextualize.

Novelty is incremental: the core idea of co-locating latency-critical and batch workloads is classical (Shenango, Caladan, REEF, SHEPHERD), and the individual mechanisms—chunked prefill (Sarathi), priority scheduling, KV swapping (vLLM), preemption points (REEF)—are largely adapted rather than new. The main contribution is the system integration and the incremental checkpointing scheme; the paper could better delineate its technical novelty relative to these works.

Several design parameters and policies lack justification or sensitivity analysis: the 8-layer preemption granularity is validated only on one small model where a single layer is a large fraction of execution time; the host memory capacity required by incremental checkpointing (which can grow with KV cache size) is not quantified; the adaptive checkpointing thresholds (50%) appear heuristic.

Presentation issues reduce polish: figure legends and text refer to the system as 'Concerto' in Figures 5-7 while the paper is titled ConServe; there are typos ('batchs', 'laod patterns', 'Upon detecting the flag is set. Workers check...'); Algorithm 2 contains an apparent dangling 'break' at Line 11; the 320GB memory is written as '320GB GB'.

Reproducibility is unclear: no code release or artifact statement is mentioned, and while the load generator is described, enough details to reproduce the trace sampling and SLO setup are not fully provided.

Fit to ICML is marginal: this is a systems paper with no methodological ML contribution; it would likely receive more expert review at a systems venue (OSDI/SOSP/MLSys), and the ML audience may find the evaluation criteria (SLO attainment, throughput) less familiar.

strengths: The problem is real and well-motivated: overprovisioning GPUs for bursty online LLM traffic while offline batch inference runs on separate clusters is a genuine inefficiency, and the paper motivates it with a real workload trace (BurstGPT) and a quantitative strawman experiment (Figure 2).

The system design is coherent and the individual mechanisms are reasonable: layer-granularity preemption with safepoints, incremental asynchronous KV-cache checkpointing to host memory amortized per decode iteration, background prefetching to hide swap-in latency, and an SLO-aware batch-size policy driven by an offline profiler. Algorithm 1/2 give a clear account of the scheduling logic.

The evaluation includes useful ablations (§6.4.1) that decompose the contribution of the SLO-aware scheduler, incremental checkpointing, and background prefetching, and a microbenchmark of the preemption safepoint overhead (§6.4.2), plus robustness experiments over load burstiness (CV) and request rates.
weaknesses: The headline claims are not supported by fair baselines. The '2.35× higher throughput than state-of-the-art online serving systems' compares ConServe against vLLM serving online requests only (zero offline throughput), which is essentially a comparison of the co-serving design against the absence of one. The '84× reduction in serving latency compared to existing co-serving systems' is measured only against vLLM++, a priority scheduler the authors implemented themselves atop vLLM 0.4.2; no actual published co-serving or priority/preemption LLM system (e.g., Llumnix, REEF/SHEPHERD-style preemption adapted to LLMs, or disaggregated baselines) is compared against.

The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the generality of the design claims. All experiments use a single model (Llama-2-7B) on a single A100-40G GPU with a vLLM 0.4.2 baseline that is dated by the time of submission. Despite the design claiming support for tensor/pipeline parallelism, multiple models, PEFT adapters, and long-context scenarios (§7), none of these are evaluated, so the discussion-section claims are speculative.

Several presentation inconsistencies undermine confidence: the legends in Figures 5, 6, and 7 label the proposed system as 'Concerto' rather than ConServe, suggesting figures were carried over from another work without careful integration. There are also numerous typos and broken sentences (e.g., '320GB GB memory', 'in batchs', 'laod patterns', 'Upon detecting the flag is set. Workers check this flag...'), and Algorithm 2 contains a 'break' on line 11 whose control flow is not clearly explained.

The paper claims 'negligible runtime overhead' for incremental checkpointing, but provides no direct measurement of the checkpointing/prefetching bandwidth consumption, host-memory footprint, or its impact on online latency under memory pressure; the host DRAM capacity required to hold checkpointed KV caches for large offline batches is never quantified, which is a central feasibility question for the design.

Reproducibility is weak: no code release is mentioned, and the evaluation depends on a specific sampling/rescaling procedure for the BurstGPT trace and self-tuned SLO thresholds (1500ms TTFT / 110ms TPOT derived from the baseline's own tail latencies), which materially shapes the headline results but is only briefly described.

There is no limitations section. The main limitations (single-GPU evaluation, dependency on accurate offline profiling, host-memory bandwidth contention between checkpointing and application I/O, fairness under mixed tenants) are either unmentioned or deferred to future work, and no research-ethics or broader-impact discussion of serving cost/reliability trade-offs is provided.

The core ideas are incremental relative to prior art: co-locating latency-critical and batch workloads with preemption is well-studied (Shenango, Caladan, REEF, SHEPHERD), and chunked prefill, continuous batching, and KV-cache swapping are inherited from vLLM/Sarathi-Serve. The novel portion reduces mainly to asynchronous incremental KV checkpointing plus a profile-driven batch-size policy, and the paper does not demonstrate why existing preemption primitives could not be extended to achieve similar results.

strengths: Addresses a practical and increasingly important problem: GPU underutilization caused by overprovisioning for bursty online LLM workloads, motivated by a real workload study (BurstGPT trace) showing minute-scale 3x load fluctuations.

The design is well-motivated and technically coherent: the three components (layer-granularity preemption, incremental KV-cache checkpointing with asynchronous swap I/O, and SLO-aware profiling-based batch sizing) each address a clearly articulated challenge, and the resume-strategy comparison in Figure 4 is a nice, intuitive framing of the design space.
Solid implementation effort (4165 LOC atop vLLM 0.4.2, safepoint instrumentation, dual CUDA streams, extended page table), described in enough detail to assess feasibility.

Reasonably thorough evaluation: end-to-end comparison on a real trace, ON/OFF phased stress tests, robustness sweeps over burstiness (CV) and request rate, and a component-wise ablation (Figure 8) that quantifies each optimization's contribution (e.g., checkpointing and prefetching recover 14.0% and 13.6% of throughput).
The drill-down on preemption overhead (988us per safepoint, 5.41ms preemption response time, 4% instrumentation cost) gives concrete evidence for the responsiveness claims.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation generality: all experiments use a single model (Llama-2-7B, FP16) on a single A100-40G. Tensor and pipeline parallelism are claimed in Section 4.3/5 but never evaluated; the multi-GPU synchronization, distributed barrier, and NCCL flag broadcast mechanisms central to the design are essentially unvalidated.

Baseline strength is a concern. Headline claims (2.35x throughput, 84x tail-latency reduction) are measured against vLLM++, a strawman that eagerly batches and swaps offline requests. There is no comparison against SLO-aware systems such as Sarathi-Serve, nor against disaggregated serving (DistServe/Splitwise) that the paper itself argues is the operators' current alternative; the 84x figure risks overstating the practical gap.

Presentation sloppiness undermines confidence: Figures 5, 6, and 7 label the proposed system as "Concerto" rather than ConServe, suggesting the evaluation was reused from a different system or an earlier manuscript without careful checking. There are also typos ("laod patterns," "batchs," inconsistent Figure 5/7 panel labeling) and the abstract's SLO numbers (110ms TPOT) differ from the 100ms example in Section 2.2 without explanation.

The SLO-aware scheduler depends on an offline profiler with static execution-time estimates; the paper does not characterize sensitivity to profiling error, workload drift (e.g., different output-length distributions than profiled), or how estimates hold under the O(n^2) attention effects the paper itself flags. TTFT prediction in Algorithm 2 rests on these estimates but error bounds are not reported.
Statistical rigor is thin: p99 latency numbers from single trace replays are reported without repetitions, variance bands, or confidence intervals, which matters for tail-latency claims.

No explicit limitations section; host-memory capacity as a scaling constraint (checkpointed KV caches of many concurrent offline requests can exceed DRAM) is not analyzed. Reproducibility is uncertain: no code or artifact release is mentioned.

Fit with the venue: this is a systems contribution with no learning-methodological novelty; while the problem is relevant to ML practitioners, the techniques (preemption, checkpointing, priority scheduling) are classical systems mechanisms, and the work would be more conventionally assessed at a systems venue.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly demonstrates (Figures 2–3) that online LLM serving overprovisions GPUs due to bursty load, and that naive preemptive co-serving yields a 3.59× TTFT and 3.01× TBT degradation plus a 4.27× offline throughput loss, clearly establishing the gap ConServe targets.

The design decomposition into three components (SLO-aware token-level scheduling, layer-wise preemption, incremental KV cache management) is coherent and each component addresses a clearly identified root cause from the motivation study; the layered safepoint mechanism with TP synchronization and CUDA Graph compatibility shows real engineering depth.

Comprehensive evaluation: three models (8B, 14B, 70B with tensor parallelism), real workload traces (BurstGPT) plus three real offline datasets, synthetic sensitivity studies over burstiness and sequence lengths, a component-by-component ablation (§6.5), and overhead microbenchmarks for both safepoints (21µs) and KV checkpointing bandwidth.

Baselines are substantive rather than strawmen: the authors extended Sarathi and DistServe schedulers into preemptive co-serving variants within the same vLLM version and tuned configurations, and they honestly report cases where baselines behave unexpectedly (e.g., Sarathi-P sometimes yielding worse TBT than Non-Preemptive due to recomputation).
weaknesses: The 'first LLM co-serving system' claim is overstated. The paper itself cites FlexLLM [42], which co-serves LLM inference and parameter-efficient fine-tuning in the same engine, and prior work on harvesting inference cycles (e.g., SpotServe [31], AntMan [65]). The related-work section asserts 'ConServe is the first to apply the principle of workload co-location specifically for LLM serving' without carefully differentiating from these systems.

A key mechanism is underspecified: Algorithm 1 signals layer-wise preemption upon a new online request, and the worker then 'resumes execution for the remainder of the iteration with only the online requests.' However, the online request was not part of the in-flight batch, so how its KV cache, attention metadata, and batch state are initialized to join mid-iteration is never explained. This is central to whether the low preemption-latency claim actually translates into low TTFT.

The latency model (Equation with k1–k5 terms) is coarse: it assumes standard dense attention quadratic scaling, omits GQA/KV-cache sharing effects, MoE routing, speculative decoding, and prefix-cache hits, and the claimed <4% prediction error is reported only as a summary number without error distribution or out-of-distribution validation. Since all scheduling decisions hinge on this model, its robustness bounds the credibility of the SLO-adherence results.

SLO 'guarantees' are overstated: ConServe achieves >99% attainment only when slack s>1, and at the strictest setting (s=1.0) still violates 14% of the time. The system provides statistical P99 attainment relative to Online-Only latencies, not hard guarantees, and the abstract/introduction language ('strong online latency guarantees') does not reflect this. There is also no explicit limitations section.

Fairness concerns in the evaluation setup: SLOs for all systems are derived from Online-Only P99 latencies, and ConServe is the only system aware of the SLO target, so the attainment metric structurally favors it; the DistServe-P baseline is a re-implementation inside vLLM rather than the original disaggregated system, and the reported sensitivity of its performance to prefill:decode ratios suggests the port may under-represent the original design.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or profile release is mentioned, and several implementation-critical details (e.g., the gather kernel semantics, page-table extension, exact profiler grid, per-model coefficient values) are absent, making independent reproduction difficult.

Minor presentation issues: Figure 2's dual y-axis is confusing (utilization defined relative to max load rather than measured GPU utilization), Table 2's column grouping is hard to parse, and some prose inconsistencies (e.g., '2.2×' in the abstract vs. '2.23×/3.00×' in evaluation) suggest the headline numbers aggregate different experimental settings without clear definition.

strengths: The paper targets a real and practically important problem: LLM inference clusters are heavily overprovisioned due to bursty online load, and the motivation is supported by concrete profiling (Figure 2, Figure 3) quantifying both GPU idleness and the 3x latency / 4x throughput degradation of naive co-serving.

The three techniques (SLO-aware token-level scheduling with a context-aware polynomial latency model, layer-wise preemption via safepoints, and incremental per-token KV cache checkpointing) form a coherent design that directly addresses the three diagnosed root causes; the mapping between motivation, design, and evaluation is clear.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: three models (8B, 14B, 70B with tensor parallelism), synthetic workloads with varying request rate, SLO slack, burstiness (CV), and input/output lengths, plus real-world workloads (BurstGPT, DuReader, MultiNews, VCSUM), and four baselines including a disaggregated architecture.

An ablation study (Section 6.5) quantifies each component's contribution, and overhead analyses for the safepoint mechanism (21us/167us) and KV checkpointing bandwidth are provided, which supports the feasibility claims.
The writing and figures are generally clear, and the system is implemented atop vLLM 0.8.4 with a substantial engineering effort (~9k lines).
weaknesses: The novelty claim of being 'the first LLM co-serving system' is overstated. The paper itself cites FlexLLM [42], which co-serves LLM inference and parameter-efficient finetuning in the same engine, yet ConServe is not compared against it. Given that FlexLLM addresses a very similar resource-harvesting problem with fine-grained scheduling and preemption, the absence of this head-to-head comparison undermines the central originality and comparative claims.

The technical components are largely incremental combinations of known ideas: the performance model is a standard roofline-style polynomial fit; layer-wise preemption resembles safepoint designs in prior DNN serving systems (REEF, PipeSwitch); incremental KV swapping is close to vLLM's existing swap mechanism applied at finer granularity. The ML-relevant contribution for an ICML audience is thin — this is primarily a systems paper.

The core evaluation relies heavily on synthetic Gamma-process workloads with a single parameterization (4096 input / 256 output tokens) for the main results; the 'real-world' evaluation uses only a 10-minute trace sample of BurstGPT. Given the paper's motivation rests on long-horizon load variability (Figure 1a covers 24 hours), the evaluation does not demonstrate the claimed harvesting benefit over realistic diurnal load cycles.

Reproducibility is questionable: no code or artifact release is mentioned, the cost model coefficients and profiling grids are under-specified, and the SLO-attainment metric depends on system-dependent P99 baselines that other groups cannot easily reproduce.

Several design limitations are not adequately addressed: the latency model assumes dense transformer attention and would need revalidation for MoE, prefix caching, or speculative decoding, all common in modern serving; host-memory growth of incremental checkpointing for long-running offline jobs is only briefly discussed; and the choice of 16-token checkpoint granularity (tied to vLLM page size) may not generalize across engines.

Some reported numbers are inconsistent or hard to verify: the abstract claims 2.2x throughput and 2.9x tail latency improvements, but Section 6.2 reports 3.00x throughput and 2.37x/2.72x latency reductions, and Table 2 reports yet different averages (2.23x throughput, 2.04x/2.86x latency), leaving the headline claims ambiguous.

There is no explicit limitations section or discussion of when co-serving would not be beneficial (e.g., saturated clusters, very tight SLOs with s=1.0, or offline workloads incompatible with shared engines).

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly demonstrates GPU underutilization from bursty LLM traffic (Figures 1-2) and quantifies why naive co-serving fails (3x latency increase, 4x throughput drop in Section 3), grounding the design in measured root causes rather than conjecture.

The three techniques are coherent and address the three identified root causes (scheduling, preemption, state management). The context-aware performance model (Latency(P,C) polynomial with <4% prediction error) is a concrete, reusable contribution, and layer-wise safepoints are carefully engineered for real deployment constraints (TP synchronization via ncclBroadcast, CUDA graph compatibility), with overheads measured (21us/safepoint, 1.1% total).

The incremental KV cache checkpointing design is a genuinely clever resolution of the swap-vs-recompute dilemma, exploiting the append-only/immutable property of KV caches; the cost analysis (349K tokens/s transfer, 10ms for a 2048-token chunk, hidden by overlap) is concrete and verified empirically.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: three models including a 70B TP=4 configuration, four diverse baselines including a disaggregated-architecture baseline (DistServe-P) and both latency- and throughput-optimal upper bounds, real-world traces (BurstGPT) plus three offline datasets, sensitivity to burstiness and request lengths, and a component-by-component ablation quantifying each technique's contribution.

The ablation (Section 6.5) and drill-down measurements (safepoint cost, KV transfer bandwidth scaling to 132GB/s in TP) give credible mechanistic support for the design decisions rather than only end-to-end wins.
weaknesses: The claim of being 'the first LLM co-serving system' is overstated: FlexLLM [42] (cited by the authors) already co-serves LLM inference with parameter-efficient finetuning in the same engine, which is conceptually very close; the paper should differentiate its contribution more precisely rather than claim primacy.

No code release or artifact statement is mentioned. Given the 9,169-line implementation atop vLLM 0.8.4 and the many tuned baseline extensions, reproducibility and independent verification rely entirely on the manuscript's description.

All experiments are on a single DGX node; the co-serving opportunity is arguably most valuable at cluster scale (multi-replica scheduling, load balancing interacting with co-serving), which is not explored. The paper also lacks an explicit limitations section.

All preemptive baselines (Sarathi-P, DistServe-P) are author-extended implementations; while porting to a common vLLM version is fair in principle, baseline tuning details are thin, and there is a risk that baseline-specific optimizations (e.g., hybrid chunk sizing, KV-cache-aware admission) were not fully explored.

Offline serving is evaluated only via throughput; there is no analysis of offline job completion time distribution, starvation guarantees, or fairness across offline requests under sustained online load, which matters for the batch-API use cases motivating the work.

Under the strictest SLO setting (s=1.0), ConServe still shows at most 86% SLO attainment, so the strongest claim of 'strict SLO guarantees' holds only with some slack; the abstract-level summary numbers (2.9x tail latency, 2.2x throughput) also do not exactly match the per-section averages (e.g., 3.00x throughput in Section 6.2, 2.23x in Section 6.3), suggesting selective aggregation.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('conefficients', 'Non-premptive'), Figure 8/9 axis labels, and the interaction of the performance model with speculative decoding or heterogeneous hardware is not addressed, limiting generality of the cost model.
